strong.text: You handled this topic well. Your answers show you attach site, test, timing and operation to the reasoning behind them, not to loose labels. Before the exam, run the review cards once so the PYQ-versus-current-practice contrasts stay sharp.

mixed.text: Some of this topic is solid and some is not yet. Perforated ulcer is mostly a set of qualifiers: most common versus always, first versus best, sealed versus free. The objectives below show which qualifiers slipped. Start the review cards with the ones marked as gaps.

weak.text: Several core areas need another pass, which is normal for a topic packed with look-alikes. Do not reread everything. Work through the review cards in the order listed, starting with confident errors, then gaps, and ask of each stem which qualifier it is testing.

secure.text: Site and wall-to-outcome are secure: you tied anterior duodenum to perforation and posterior to gastroduodenal artery bleeding.

shaky.text: Site and wall-to-outcome are partly there. Anchor it: the anterior wall faces the free peritoneal cavity, the posterior wall faces the gastroduodenal artery. Revisit the O1 card.

gap.text: The anterior-versus-posterior duodenum pairing is still unstable. Rebuild it from what lies behind each wall, then redo the O1 card.

secure.text: You separated true free gas from Chilaiditi pseudo-pneumoperitoneum, and kept 'most common cause' as a frequency, not a rule.

shaky.text: Free gas versus Chilaiditi is only partly secure. Check haustra and the patient, not just the location under the dome. Redo the O2 card.

gap.text: Gas under the right dome is still being read by location alone. Contrast the true signs with Chilaiditi (colon with haustra between liver and diaphragm), then redo the O2 card.

secure.text: You read the clinical course well: sudden pain, a patient lying still, and the false-calm reaction stage before bacterial peritonitis.

shaky.text: The clinical picture is partly secure. Trace the sequence once more: chemical peritonitis, apparent improvement, then bacterial peritonitis. Redo the O3 card.

gap.text: The course of the disease is running the wrong way in your model: feeling better is not getting better. Trace chemical, reaction, then bacterial peritonitis, and redo the O3 card.

secure.text: You kept first investigation and most sensitive investigation as two questions, and held PYQ and current-practice frames apart.

shaky.text: First versus most sensitive test is partly secure. Name which question the stem asks before choosing. Redo the O4 card.

gap.text: One test is still serving every 'which investigation' stem. Learn the ladder: erect X-ray first, CT most sensitive, and note what PYQs expected. Redo the O4 card.

secure.text: You treated a clear film or a soft abdomen as not excluding perforation, especially in elderly or steroid-treated patients.

shaky.text: What a clear film or soft abdomen excludes is partly secure. Neither rules perforation out, and a quarter of films show no gas. Redo the O5 card.

gap.text: A clear film or soft abdomen is still reassuring you too much. Gas shows in only about three-quarters of films, and steroids and age blunt signs. Redo the O5 card; this one is a safety habit.

secure.text: View and contrast choices are secure: left lateral decubitus if the patient cannot sit, about 10 minutes upright, Gastrografin not barium.

shaky.text: View, timing and contrast are partly secure. Derive each from the mechanism: where gas rises, how long it takes, what leaks into the peritoneum. Redo the O6 card.

gap.text: View, timing or contrast still comes from habit. Derive them: gas needs about 10 minutes to rise, left decubitus lets the liver outline it, and barium causes peritonitis. Redo the O6 card.

secure.text: You put resuscitation, antibiotics and PPI ahead of theatre in a shocked patient.

shaky.text: The order of care in a shocked patient is partly secure. Ask what keeps the patient alive to reach anaesthesia. Redo the O7 card.

gap.text: Theatre is still going first in your sequence. Fluids, NG tube, antibiotics and PPI come before the operation. Redo the O7 card and rehearse the order aloud.

secure.text: You chose omental patch closure with lavage and mapped the exam name to the strict one.

shaky.text: The operation and patch names are partly secure. Graham is a free plug and Cellan-Jones a pedicled tongue, though PYQs key 'Graham's patch'. Redo the O8 card.

gap.text: The two patch names are still tangled. Graham: free omental plug. Cellan-Jones: pedicled tongue. PYQs key Graham's patch. Redo the O8 card.

secure.text: You chose patch closure, eradication and PPI over routine vagotomy, and added biopsy for a gastric ulcer.

shaky.text: Post-repair care and the gastric addition are partly secure. Recheck the modern logic and remember the biopsy step for gastric ulcers. Redo the O9 card.

gap.text: Old acid-surgery logic or a missed gastric biopsy is still showing. Current practice is patch plus H. pylori eradication and PPI, and a gastric ulcer needs biopsy for carcinoma. Redo the O9 card.

secure.text: You attached the right condition to Taylor management: selected stable patients with a sealed perforation shown on contrast.

shaky.text: When Taylor management applies is partly secure. The qualifier is sealed, confirmed on Gastrografin, and stable. Redo the O10 card.

gap.text: Taylor is still a name without its condition. It is for a sealed perforation confirmed on contrast in a stable patient, not any stable patient. Redo the O10 card.

secure.text: You recalled the three Boey factors and their thresholds.

shaky.text: The Boey score is partly secure. Rebuild three items: shock (systolic under 100), major illness, delay over 24 hours. Age is not one. Redo the O11 card.

gap.text: The Boey score is padded or has the wrong thresholds. Rebuild it as shock under 100 mmHg, major co-existing illness, delay over 24 hours. Redo the O11 card.

secure.text: Eponyms and risk factors held up: Cushing with brain, Curling with burns, Kehr with spleen.

shaky.text: Eponyms are partly secure. Anchor Cushing to the brain and keep Kehr with splenic rupture. Redo the O12 card.

gap.text: Eponyms are still swapping. Cushing goes with head injury, Curling with burns, Kehr with spleen, Valentino with the appendicitis mimic. Redo the O12 card.

avoided.text: You tied each wall to what lies behind it.

fell_recovered.text: You swapped the walls at first, then held the pairing. Under pressure the labels can flip back: ask what lies behind the wall (free peritoneum in front, gastroduodenal artery behind).

fell_open.text: Your model: posterior is the deep, dangerous wall, so it perforates. You may have fixed it on the spot, so meet it again on a fresh question in the review card: anterior perforates, posterior bleeds.

avoided.text: You kept 'most common cause' as a frequency.

fell_recovered.text: You first read 'most common' as 'always', then corrected it. Under time pressure the word drops out again. Check for a non-ulcer cause of free gas.

fell_open.text: Your model: free gas always means perforated ulcer. You may have corrected it on the spot, so meet it on a fresh counter-case in the review card, such as gas after recent laparoscopy.

avoided.text: You checked what the gas sat in, not just where.

fell_recovered.text: You first diagnosed by location, then switched to checking haustra and the patient. Re-check this when a right-dome film looks classic.

fell_open.text: Your model: any gas under the right dome is free gas. You may have corrected this on the spot, so test it again on the review card: Chilaiditi has colon with haustra and a well patient.

avoided.text: You separated first test from most sensitive test.

fell_recovered.text: You first used one ranking for every test question, then split first from best. Ask which question the stem poses each time.

fell_open.text: Your model: one test answers every 'which investigation' stem. You may have corrected this on the spot, so meet it again in the review card: erect X-ray first, CT most sensitive.

avoided.text: You held the PYQ key and current practice apart.

fell_recovered.text: You first gave one answer for both frames, then separated them. Name the frame before answering, especially on exam keys.

fell_open.text: Your model: the exam key and current practice always agree. You may have corrected this on the spot, so revisit the review card: PYQs expected erect X-ray, current practice favours CT for sensitivity.

avoided.text: You did not let a clear film close the question.

fell_recovered.text: You first read no gas as no perforation, then corrected. Under pressure this habit returns; with peritonitis signs and a clear film, think CT.

fell_open.text: Your model: a clear erect film excludes perforation. You may have corrected this on the spot, so meet it on a fresh question in the review card. About a quarter of perforations show no gas, so a clear film is unsafe to trust.

avoided.text: You adjusted the view to the patient's posture.

fell_recovered.text: You first picked a habitual view, then derived the right one. Re-derive it from where gas rises when the patient cannot sit.

fell_open.text: Your model: the usual textbook view, or a supine or right-sided film, works for a patient who cannot sit. You may have corrected this on the spot, so revisit the review card: left lateral decubitus, liver outlining the gas.

avoided.text: You allowed time for gas to rise.

fell_recovered.text: You first assumed gas rises at once, then fixed the timing. Remember the mechanism: gas needs about 10 minutes upright to reach the diaphragm.

fell_open.text: Your model: gas moves instantly, so the film can be taken at once. You may have corrected this on the spot, so meet it again in the review card: about 10 minutes upright.

avoided.text: You resuscitated before theatre.

fell_recovered.text: You first put surgery ahead of fluids, then re-ordered. Under exam pressure the definitive step tends to jump the queue; resuscitate first.

fell_open.text: Your model: the operation is the first step because it is the definitive treatment. You may have corrected this on the spot, so meet the order again in the review card: fluids and NG tube, antibiotics and PPI, then theatre.

avoided.text: You checked the Taylor qualifier.

fell_recovered.text: You first applied Taylor to a stable patient, then added the condition. Ask each time: sealed, confirmed on contrast, and selected?

fell_open.text: Your model: Taylor management suits any stable patient. You may have corrected this on the spot, so meet it in the review card: free perforation with generalised peritonitis needs surgery, and Taylor needs a confirmed seal.

avoided.text: You mapped the exam name to the strict name.

fell_recovered.text: You first treated the two patch names as interchangeable, then separated them. Keep both in mind: PYQs key Graham's patch, strictly Cellan-Jones is pedicled.

fell_open.text: Your model: Graham and Cellan-Jones are the same or interchangeable. You may have corrected this on the spot, so revisit the review card: Graham free plug, Cellan-Jones pedicled tongue, and PYQs key Graham's patch.

avoided.text: You chose current practice over old acid surgery.

fell_recovered.text: You first reached for vagotomy or gastrectomy, then switched. Older PYQs still list them; current practice is patch plus eradication and PPI.

fell_open.text: Your model: acid-reducing surgery belongs in every ulcer operation. You may have corrected this on the spot, so meet it again in the review card: patch closure, H. pylori eradication and PPI.

avoided.text: You paired the stress-ulcer eponyms correctly.

fell_recovered.text: You first swapped the pair, then fixed it. Anchor it: Cushing goes with the brain, Curling with burns.

fell_open.text: Your model: the eponym pair is order-based, so Curling and Cushing swap. You may have corrected this on the spot, so revisit the review card: Cushing with brain, Curling with burns.

avoided.text: You paired each eponym with its own disease.

fell_recovered.text: You first followed the shared shoulder-tip pain to the wrong eponym, then corrected. Ask which disease owns each eponym.

fell_open.text: Your model: shoulder-tip pain points to Kehr's sign for perforation. You may have corrected this on the spot, so meet it in the review card: Kehr belongs to splenic rupture, and Valentino's is the appendicitis mimic.

avoided.text: You recognised the reaction stage as false calm.

fell_recovered.text: You first read the lull as recovery, then fixed it. Late presenters who look better are the ones who catch people out; the lull comes before bacterial peritonitis.

fell_open.text: Your model: feeling better means getting better. You may have corrected this on the spot, so meet it again in the review card: chemical peritonitis, reaction as dilution, then bacterial peritonitis.

avoided.text: You read the still patient as peritonitis.

fell_recovered.text: You first reversed the movement sign, then traced the mechanism. Movement jars an inflamed peritoneum, whereas colic eases with moving.

fell_open.text: Your model: worse pain means more movement. You may have corrected this on the spot, so meet it again in the review card: peritonitis lies still, colic writhes.

avoided.text: You added the biopsy for a gastric ulcer.

fell_recovered.text: You first closed a gastric ulcer like a duodenal one, then added the biopsy. Keep it as a cue when the stem mentions weight loss.

fell_open.text: Your model: all perforations are closed the same way. You may have corrected this on the spot, so meet it in the review card: a perforated gastric ulcer needs biopsy or excision to exclude carcinoma.

avoided.text: You chose the contrast by what it does after a leak.

fell_recovered.text: You first reached for barium, then switched. Ask what the medium does in the peritoneum.

fell_open.text: Your model: barium is the best contrast for any GI question. You may have corrected this on the spot, so revisit the review card: Gastrografin shows sealing, and barium is contraindicated because it causes severe peritonitis.

avoided.text: You recalled the three Boey items.

fell_recovered.text: You first added extra mortality factors or borrowed thresholds, then rebuilt it. Three items: shock, major illness, delay.

fell_open.text: Your model: Boey includes every known mortality factor, with thresholds borrowed from other scores. You may have corrected this on the spot, so meet it again in the review card: shock under 100 mmHg, major illness, delay over 24 hours.

avoided.text: You did not wait for rigidity.

fell_recovered.text: You first trusted a soft abdomen, then recognised masking. Elderly or steroid-treated patients may never show board-like rigidity.

fell_open.text: Your model: no rigidity rules out perforation. You may have corrected this on the spot, so meet it in the review card: age and steroids blunt signs, so image on suspicion.

E1.text: You tend to match look-alikes by surface cues such as position or familiarity: wall, dome, contrast. For each pair, ask what actually differs, such as what lies behind, inside versus outside bowel, or what leaks.

E2.text: You tend to pad a fixed list with familiar items or borrow figures from other lists. Rebuild the list from its logic and check each item against it.

E3.text: You tend to reverse the direction of a disease or sign: relief read as recovery, or movement read the wrong way. Predict the mechanism first, then check the sign.

E4.text: You tend to turn a frequency or a test result into an absolute: most common into always, no gas into no perforation. Look for the qualifier and ask for a counter-case.

E5.text: You tend to give one answer where the exam key and current practice differ. Name the frame in the stem first: PYQs expected one thing, current practice may favour another.

E6.text: You tend to remember a number without the mechanism that fixes it. Tie each figure to the reason behind it.

E7.text: You tend to drop the qualifier that changes the answer: setting, host or condition. Before answering, ask which condition makes this the right choice.

E8.text: You tend to use one ranking for every 'which test' question. Ask whether the stem wants first, most sensitive or investigation of choice.

E9.text: You tend to put the definitive step first, or to leave out the step that depends on the case. Order the steps by what keeps the patient safe, then add case-specific steps.

E10.text: You tend to map eponyms by a shared symptom or order of appearance. Anchor each eponym to the disease that owns it.

overconfident.text: You tapped Sure on at least two answers that were wrong. Those confident errors are the ones most worth correcting, so do their cards first. Before you tap Sure, name the qualifier that makes your answer right.

underconfident.text: You were right on several answers you marked as guesses. Your knowledge is ahead of your confidence. On the next pass, tap Sure when you can state the reason, and save Guessing for answers you cannot justify.

calibrated.text: Your Sure taps matched your answers: when you were sure you were right, and your doubts were fair. Keep checking the qualifier before you tap.

hints_heavy.text: You asked for hints or explanations often. That is fine while the material is new, but it means some right answers had help. Retry the review cards without hints to see what you hold unaided.

hints_none.text: You used no hints, so your falls are honest information, not a lack of support. Next time, try a hint after a first miss; it can show which qualifier you skipped.

hinted_only.text: For at least one objective, you were right only after a hint. Treat that objective as unproven and retry its card cold, without the hint.

fast_lane.text: You took at least one skip, such as the site, walk-through, test ladder or recap lesson. The report does not assume you earned it. Open the cards for the skipped lessons and check you can state each rule without prompting.

gap.text: Start the review cards with confident errors, then gaps, then shaky objectives. For each, find the qualifier or contrast the stem tests: first versus best, sealed versus free, exam key versus current practice. Revisit in 1 day, then 3 days.

clear.text: No gaps showed. Keep the review cards on the spaced schedule, especially the PYQ-versus-current-practice contrasts, which decay quickly, and attempt a mixed set of exam stems.
